# Abstract

This study examines the relationship between urban green spaces and mental health outcomes among city residents. As urbanization continues to accelerate globally, understanding the psychological impacts of environmental design becomes increasingly critical for public health planning. Through a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative surveys (n=312) and qualitative interviews (n=24) conducted across three metropolitan areas, this research investigates how accessibility to and frequency of green space use correlates with self-reported mental health indicators including stress levels, anxiety symptoms, and overall psychological well-being. Results indicate a statistically significant positive association between regular green space exposure and improved mental health outcomes, with participants reporting 23% lower stress scores and 18% reduced anxiety symptoms when accessing green spaces at least twice weekly. The study also identifies key mediating factors including duration of visits, types of activities engaged in, and perceived quality of green spaces. Socioeconomic variables, including income level and residential proximity to parks, emerged as important considerations affecting equitable access. Findings suggest that urban planning initiatives prioritizing accessible, well-maintained green spaces may serve as effective public health interventions for mental wellness. This research contributes to the growing body of evidence supporting nature-based solutions for urban mental health challenges and provides actionable recommendations for policymakers, urban planners, and public health officials seeking to create mentally healthier cities through evidence-based environmental design.

# Introduction

Urban environments dominate contemporary human life, with over 55% of the global population now residing in cities—a figure projected to reach 68% by 2050. While urbanization offers economic opportunities and cultural benefits, dense city living presents significant mental health challenges. Rising rates of depression, anxiety, and stress-related disorders among urban populations have prompted researchers to examine environmental factors that may buffer against these psychological risks. Among potential interventions, urban green spaces—including parks, gardens, tree-lined streets, and natural reserves—have emerged as promising elements of mentally healthy city design.
